title: Acute Asthma: Wheeze, Silence, and the Patient Who Is Tiring
bottomLine: In acute asthma, trend airflow and work of breathing—not wheeze volume alone. A quiet or silent chest, exhaustion, altered mental status, worsening hypoxemia, or a rising/normalizing PaCO2 in a patient who remains in severe distress can signal impending ventilatory failure and requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Dyspnea, cough, wheeze, prolonged expiration, chest tightness, tachypnea, and accessory-muscle use
Severe attack: difficulty speaking, poor air movement, marked retractions, agitation or drowsiness
Less wheeze is dangerous when air entry is also decreasing
assess: Position upright and assess speech, respiratory rate/effort, air entry, SpO2, heart rate, mental status, and response after each treatment
Peak flow may help quantify obstruction when the patient can perform it safely
Reassess potassium and cardiac effects when repeated high-dose beta2-agonists are used and labs/monitoring are ordered
actions: Give prescribed rapid bronchodilator therapy promptly and oxygen when hypoxemic
Administer systemic corticosteroid when ordered for a significant exacerbation
Escalate early for fatigue, worsening air entry, persistent hypoxemia, altered consciousness, or poor response
diagnostics: Blood gas testing is not routine for every mild attack; it becomes important when severe distress, fatigue, altered mental status, or ventilatory failure is suspected
Chest imaging is used when another diagnosis or complication such as pneumonia or pneumothorax is suspected
medicationSafety: Albuterol: expect tremor/tachycardia; repeated doses can lower potassium
Ipratropium: commonly added in moderate-to-severe acute exacerbations
Systemic corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation but are not the immediate bronchodilator
redFlags: Rising PaCO2 with ongoing severe distress
teaching: Reinforce controller versus reliever therapy, inhaler/spacer technique, trigger reduction, and the written asthma action plan
Frequent rescue-inhaler reliance signals poor control and needs follow-up
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN can perform focused respiratory assessment, administer ordered inhaled/systemic medications within scope, reassess response, reinforce teaching, and activate escalation. Do not independently diagnose severity or alter the long-term regimen without an order/authorized protocol.
examTrap: Assuming wheezing that becomes quieter means the patient is improving without checking air entry and effort.
oneLinePearl: A silent chest can be the loudest emergency sign in asthma.
sourceBasis: NHLBI/NAEPP Asthma Management Guidelines and 2020 Focused Updates

title: COPD Exacerbation: Oxygen, Ventilation, and the CO2 Trap
bottomLine: Treat hypoxemia in COPD; do not withhold oxygen because of the old 'hypoxic drive' myth. Use controlled oxygen to the ordered target, bronchodilators and other prescribed therapy, then reassess ventilation, mental status, work of breathing, and blood gases when hypercapnic failure is suspected.
recognize: Increased dyspnea, cough, sputum volume/purulence, wheeze, reduced breath sounds, tachypnea
Hypercapnia may present with headache, confusion, drowsiness, flushed skin, or worsening acidosis
A patient can have acceptable SpO2 while ventilation and CO2 clearance are deteriorating
assess: Compare current respiratory status and oxygen requirement with baseline
Trend respiratory effort, air entry, SpO2, mental status, heart rate, and response after bronchodilators
Watch for fatigue and inability to protect the airway
actions: Position upright and titrate prescribed oxygen rather than abruptly removing it from a hypoxemic patient
Administer ordered short-acting bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroid
Prepare for noninvasive ventilatory support/escalation when acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with acidosis and increased work of breathing persists
diagnostics: Blood gas helps evaluate acute hypercapnia/acidosis when clinical concern exists
Chest imaging helps identify pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, or another cause of worsening
Electrolytes may matter with frequent beta2-agonist use
medicationSafety: Albuterol can cause tachycardia, tremor, and hypokalemia
Ipratropium adds bronchodilation
Systemic steroids can worsen glucose control and cause mood/sleep effects
Antibiotics are indication-driven; colored sputum alone is not a universal reason for self-started antibiotics
teaching: Reinforce inhaler technique, smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/activity plan, and prescribed oxygen safety
Teach that increasing sleepiness during an exacerbation is not simply 'being tired'
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN monitors and administers ordered therapy within scope and reports deterioration promptly. Selection of ventilatory settings or independent oxygen/medication regimen changes requires the authorized clinician/protocol.
examTrap: Withholding oxygen from a hypoxemic COPD patient because oxygen is believed to 'turn off the respiratory drive.'
oneLinePearl: Give controlled oxygen for hypoxemia, then watch ventilation and mental status.

title: Pneumonia: Infection Plus Gas-Exchange Risk
bottomLine: Pneumonia becomes urgent when infection is accompanied by worsening oxygenation, sepsis, hemodynamic instability, or respiratory fatigue. Support oxygenation and secretion clearance, obtain ordered specimens/tests without unnecessary delay, give antimicrobials as ordered, and reassess whether the patient is responding.
recognize: Fever or hypothermia, cough, sputum, pleuritic pain, crackles, dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia
Older adults may present with weakness, falls, poor intake, or acute confusion rather than high fever
Deterioration can reflect sepsis, pleural infection, respiratory failure, or another diagnosis
assess: Trend SpO2, respiratory rate/effort, breath sounds, temperature, mental status, perfusion, intake/output, and ability to clear secretions
Assess swallowing/aspiration risk when the history suggests it
Monitor response after oxygen, fluids, antipyretics, bronchodilators when indicated, and antimicrobials
actions: Position to optimize ventilation and mobilize as tolerated
Administer prescribed oxygen and antimicrobials on schedule
Support hydration and airway clearance when not contraindicated
Escalate for sepsis or respiratory deterioration
diagnostics: Chest imaging supports diagnosis/extent
Cultures are obtained when ordered and clinically indicated; do not delay urgent treatment in an unstable patient solely to complete every specimen
CBC, chemistry, lactate, blood gas, or other tests depend on severity
medicationSafety: Verify allergies before antibiotics and monitor for anaphylaxis, severe diarrhea, renal effects, QT issues, or other drug-specific toxicity
Do not stop antibiotics early just because fever improves unless the treatment plan changes
redFlags: Pleural complication or rapidly worsening pain
teaching: Complete prescribed antimicrobial therapy, hydrate as appropriate, mobilize/deep breathe as instructed, avoid tobacco, and obtain recommended vaccines
Teach specific return precautions for worsening breathlessness, confusion, cyanosis, or inability to maintain intake
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN priorities are focused assessment, ordered treatment, airway/comfort care, monitoring for sepsis or respiratory failure, and escalation—not independently choosing the antimicrobial regimen.
examTrap: Focusing on fever reduction while missing rising oxygen need, hypotension, or acute confusion.
oneLinePearl: With pneumonia, the dangerous question is not 'Is there a fever?' but 'Is gas exchange or perfusion failing?'

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Sudden Dyspnea After a Clot-Risk Story
bottomLine: Sudden unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, syncope, or hypoxemia in a patient with VTE risk should trigger urgent assessment and escalation for possible pulmonary embolism. Hypotension, severe hypoxemia, altered mental status, or shock indicates high-risk deterioration.
recognize: Risk: recent surgery/immobility, prior VTE, active cancer, estrogen exposure, pregnancy/postpartum, major trauma, or thrombophilia
Possible presentation: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, anxiety, hemoptysis, syncope
Massive/high-risk PE can cause acute right-heart strain, hypotension, obstructive shock, or arrest
assess: Assess ABCs, SpO2, respiratory effort, blood pressure/perfusion, mental status, chest pain, and DVT signs
Keep an unstable patient monitored and limit unnecessary exertion
Monitor closely for bleeding after anticoagulation or thrombolytic therapy
actions: Provide ordered oxygen/support and activate urgent evaluation
Administer prescribed anticoagulation when ordered and not contraindicated
Prepare for higher-acuity reperfusion/emergency therapy when hemodynamic instability is present
diagnostics: CT pulmonary angiography is commonly used when appropriate; V/Q testing is used in selected patients
D-dimer is a rule-out tool only in appropriate probability settings and is not a stand-alone diagnosis
ECG, troponin/BNP, echo, and ultrasound may help assess strain/source/severity
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants prevent extension/new clot but create bleeding risk
Thrombolytics can cause major or intracranial bleeding and require strict screening/monitoring
teaching: Reinforce anticoagulant adherence and bleeding precautions
Teach VTE prevention through mobility, hydration when appropriate, and prescribed prophylaxis during high-risk periods
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes the pattern, supports oxygenation/circulation, administers ordered medications within scope, monitors bleeding and response, and escalates. Diagnostic probability scoring and reperfusion selection are provider/team decisions.
examTrap: Sending a suddenly dyspneic postoperative patient to walk to the bathroom or waiting for a routine chest x-ray before escalating instability.
oneLinePearl: Sudden dyspnea plus clot risk is PE until the team safely rules it out.
sourceBasis: CHEST Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease Guideline

title: Pneumothorax and Chest Tubes: Protect the One-Way Exit
bottomLine: A chest drainage system must remain patent, closed, upright, and below chest level. New severe dyspnea, unilateral absent breath sounds, hypotension, distended neck veins, rapidly expanding subcutaneous emphysema, or abrupt clinical deterioration can signal tension physiology or drainage failure and requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Pneumothorax: sudden dyspnea/pleuritic pain, reduced breath sounds, possible hypoxemia
Tension physiology: severe distress plus impaired perfusion such as hypotension/tachycardia and possible JVD
Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber may indicate an air leak; expected patterns depend on the device and clinical context
assess: Assess respiratory effort, SpO2, bilateral breath sounds, insertion site, dressing, tubing, drainage amount/character, and the drainage unit
Check for kinks, dependent loops, disconnection, or a tipped system
Mark/trend drainage according to policy and report sudden large or bloody changes
actions: Keep the system below chest level and tubing unobstructed
If disconnected, re-establish a sterile closed system promptly according to emergency policy
If the tube is pulled from the patient, apply the facility-specified emergency dressing and escalate immediately
Do not routinely clamp, strip, or milk the tube
diagnostics: Chest imaging may confirm tube/lung status, but an unstable patient with tension physiology requires emergency treatment without waiting for routine imaging
medicationSafety: Provide ordered analgesia while continuing respiratory assessment; pain control should support breathing/coughing without causing unsafe oversedation
redFlags: Hypotension with unilateral absent breath sounds
teaching: Teach the patient to avoid pulling/kinking tubing and to report sudden dyspnea, chest pain, or new bubbling/leaking concerns
Encourage breathing/mobility activities as ordered while protecting the system
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN can monitor and maintain a chest drainage system according to state/facility scope, but chest-tube insertion/removal, clamping decisions, and advanced troubleshooting may be restricted. Escalate unexpected changes rather than improvising.
examTrap: Clamping a chest tube routinely during transport or because bubbling is seen, potentially trapping air in the pleural space.
oneLinePearl: Chest tube: closed, below, unkinked—and never routinely clamped.

title: ARDS: Refractory Hypoxemia and Lung-Protective Support
bottomLine: ARDS is acute diffuse inflammatory lung injury with severe gas-exchange failure. The PN/LVN priority is to recognize increasing oxygen/ventilatory support needs, monitor response and complications of lung-protective treatment, provide meticulous supportive care, and escalate deterioration—not independently change ventilator strategy.
recognize: Acute hypoxemia after a major insult such as sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, or pancreatitis
Diffuse bilateral lung opacities and worsening oxygenation not fully explained by simple fluid overload
Increasing work of breathing may progress to mechanical ventilation
assess: Trend SpO2, respiratory effort, ventilator/oxygen-device status, breath sounds, hemodynamics, mental status, urine output, and skin integrity
Assess for ventilator-associated complications and intolerance of prone positioning when used
Monitor fluid balance because both underperfusion and fluid overload can worsen outcomes
actions: Maintain prescribed oxygen/ventilatory support and immediately troubleshoot obvious equipment disconnection while calling for help
Cluster care and reduce unnecessary oxygen demand in severe instability
Implement oral care, VTE/pressure-injury prevention, mobility/turning plan, and aspiration precautions as ordered
Assist safely with prone-position protocols when trained and assigned
diagnostics: Blood gases and oxygenation trends help evaluate gas exchange
Imaging and clinical data help distinguish ARDS from cardiogenic pulmonary edema and other causes
Do not interpret a single SpO2 without considering device settings and trajectory
medicationSafety: Sedatives/analgesics used during ventilation can cause hypotension and prolonged sedation; monitor closely
Neuromuscular blockade requires deep sedation/analgesia and intensive monitoring when used—paralysis does not provide sedation
redFlags: Ventilator disconnect or high-pressure alarm with distress
teaching: Explain equipment and care in simple language to the patient/family and reinforce that recovery may be gradual
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN monitors the patient and ordered respiratory support within authorized setting/scope, reports alarms and deterioration, and performs assigned supportive care. Independent ventilator setting changes are not assumed.
examTrap: Silencing a ventilator alarm or increasing oxygen/pressure without first assessing the patient and identifying the cause within the authorized protocol.
oneLinePearl: ARDS care is trend + support + complication prevention; unexplained desaturation is never 'just the machine.'
sourceBasis: American Thoracic Society ARDS clinical practice guideline

title: Respiratory Failure and ABGs: Oxygenation Is Not Ventilation
bottomLine: A normal pulse oximeter does not prove adequate ventilation. Hypoxemic failure is primarily an oxygenation problem; hypercapnic failure is a ventilation problem. Rising PaCO2 with acidemia, fatigue, or declining mental status signals inadequate ventilation and requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Hypoxemia: low oxygen saturation/PaO2 with dyspnea, agitation, cyanosis or confusion
Hypercapnia: headache, flushed skin, confusion, somnolence, asterixis, and respiratory acidosis
Compensation patterns depend on whether the disorder is acute or chronic
assess: Assess respiratory rate/effort, depth, air entry, mental status, SpO2, oxygen device, and sedating medications
Trend ABGs with the clinical picture rather than memorizing one isolated value
Review whether the patient is tiring despite apparently slower respirations
actions: Support airway/oxygenation and administer ordered therapy
Reverse or address a reversible cause such as opioid effect when an authorized protocol/order exists
Escalate for worsening acidemia, hypercapnia, hypoxemia, or inability to protect the airway
diagnostics: ABG interpretation sequence: pH -> PaCO2 respiratory direction -> HCO3 metabolic direction -> compensation -> oxygenation
Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation but does not measure PaCO2
medicationSafety: Opioids, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives can depress ventilation; monitor respiratory status and level of consciousness, especially when combined or in high-risk patients
teaching: Teach patients using sedating medications to follow dosing instructions and avoid unapproved combinations with alcohol or other sedatives
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN can recognize abnormal blood-gas patterns and report clinical significance, but should not independently diagnose the underlying respiratory disorder or change ventilator settings unless an authorized protocol specifically permits it.
examTrap: Assuming a SpO2 of 96% rules out respiratory failure in a somnolent patient receiving supplemental oxygen who is hypoventilating.
oneLinePearl: SpO2 tells you oxygenation; CO2 and mental status tell you ventilation.

title: Oxygen Devices: Choose the Ordered Support, Then Reassess the Patient
bottomLine: Oxygen is a medication/therapy: verify the device and ordered target, apply it correctly, assess skin/fire safety, and reassess the patient's saturation, respiratory effort, and mental status. A worsening patient needs escalation even if the device is functioning perfectly.
recognize: Nasal cannula provides low-to-moderate supplemental oxygen for many stable patients
Simple masks require sufficient flow to avoid rebreathing exhaled CO2
Venturi-style devices provide more controlled oxygen concentration
Nonrebreather masks can deliver high inspired oxygen when the reservoir remains appropriately inflated and flow is adequate
assess: Check SpO2 trend, respiratory effort, device fit, tubing, oxygen source, humidification when indicated, skin pressure points, and mental status
Confirm the patient's prescribed target rather than assuming every patient should be driven to 100% saturation
Validate an unexpected pulse-ox reading by assessing perfusion, probe placement, motion, and the patient
actions: Apply the ordered device and flow/concentration correctly
Address obvious equipment failure immediately
Escalate when oxygen need rises, work of breathing worsens, or the patient cannot maintain the target
diagnostics: Pulse oximetry can be affected by poor perfusion, motion, nail products, dyshemoglobinemia, and other factors; correlate with the clinical picture and blood gas when ordered
medicationSafety: Oxygen supports combustion: keep it away from smoking, flames, sparks, and petroleum-based products not approved for oxygen use
redFlags: New cyanosis or altered mental status
Device disconnection in a dependent patient
teaching: No smoking or open flame around oxygen
Use home oxygen only at prescribed settings unless instructed by the authorized care team
Protect tubing from trip hazards
scopeAndDelegation: Oxygen titration authority varies by order/protocol and setting. The PN/LVN may apply and monitor oxygen as authorized, but should escalate rising requirements rather than independently escalating through advanced devices outside scope.
examTrap: Treating the pulse-ox number instead of the patient or setting every patient's oxygen goal to 100%.
oneLinePearl: Right device, right target, reassess the person—not just the number.

title: Tracheostomy and Suctioning: Airway First, Sterility and Technique Matter
bottomLine: Suction because assessment shows retained secretions—not simply because a clock says so. Use the prescribed sterile/clean technique for the setting, preoxygenate when indicated, limit suction trauma, and stop/escalate for severe hypoxemia, bradycardia, airway loss, or inability to pass the catheter.
recognize: Need for suction may include visible/audible secretions, coarse breath sounds, increased work of breathing, declining oxygenation, ineffective cough, or ventilator signs consistent with secretion obstruction
Fresh tracheostomies and accidental decannulation can become airway emergencies
Excessive or prolonged suction can cause hypoxemia, mucosal trauma, dysrhythmia, and bronchospasm
assess: Assess respiratory effort, breath sounds, SpO2, secretion amount/character, cough effectiveness, trach position/ties, stoma, and emergency equipment
Confirm inner cannula and humidification care according to the specific device
Reassess after suction rather than assuming secretion removal was adequate
actions: Use aseptic technique appropriate to open suction and facility policy
Apply suction only during catheter withdrawal and keep passes brief according to protocol
Allow oxygenation/recovery between passes
Keep emergency tracheostomy equipment available as required for the setting
diagnostics: New bloody secretions, persistent obstruction, fever, or respiratory decline may require further evaluation; do not repeatedly suction a problem that is not resolving
medicationSafety: Avoid routine saline instillation into the airway unless specifically ordered/indicated by protocol; it can worsen oxygenation and does not replace adequate humidification
teaching: Teach trach care, humidification, secretion management, emergency contacts, and signs of obstruction/infection according to the home-care plan
scopeAndDelegation: Tracheostomy suctioning and tube-care authority depends on state/facility policy and competency validation. Airway deterioration always requires immediate escalation regardless of who normally performs the procedure.
examTrap: Deep, repeated suctioning on a fixed schedule despite no clinical indication, causing hypoxemia and trauma.
oneLinePearl: Assess, suction briefly when needed, oxygenate, reassess.

title: Mechanical Ventilation: When the Alarm Is the Patient Calling
bottomLine: When a ventilator alarm sounds, assess the patient first. High-pressure alarms commonly point to resistance/obstruction problems; low-pressure alarms often suggest leak/disconnection. If the patient is unstable and the ventilator problem cannot be rapidly corrected, call for help and use the emergency ventilation plan rather than silencing the alarm.
recognize: High pressure: secretions, coughing, biting, bronchospasm, kinked tubing, water in circuit, reduced lung compliance, pneumothorax
Low pressure/low exhaled volume: disconnection, cuff/circuit leak, tube displacement
Sudden desaturation can be patient, airway, ventilator, or oxygen-source failure
assess: Look at the patient: chest rise, breath sounds, SpO2, heart rate, blood pressure, mental status/sedation
Trace the airway/circuit from patient to machine for obvious disconnection or obstruction
Assess tube position markers and secretions according to policy
actions: Correct simple visible problems immediately when within role
Suction when assessment indicates secretion obstruction
Activate respiratory therapy/RN/provider/emergency support for instability
Use bag-mask/manual ventilation with the prescribed oxygen source if required by the emergency protocol and trained/authorized
diagnostics: Blood gases, chest imaging, and ventilator data may be used to evaluate deterioration, but do not delay emergency response to airway/ventilation failure
medicationSafety: Sedation/analgesia require ongoing assessment for hypotension, oversedation, delirium, and withdrawal; paralysis does not equal sedation
teaching: Explain alarms and procedures to awake patients and use communication aids when intubation prevents speech
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN care of mechanically ventilated patients varies by setting and state. Do not assume independent authority to change ventilator modes, PEEP, tidal volume, or advanced settings; assess, address immediate authorized safety problems, and escalate.
examTrap: Pressing silence repeatedly or changing ventilator settings before assessing the patient and circuit.
oneLinePearl: Alarm = patient first, circuit second, silence last.
sourceBasis: AARC mechanical-ventilation and artificial-airway practice guidance

title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Airborne Precautions Before Confirmation
bottomLine: Suspected infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB requires prompt airborne infection-control measures while evaluation is underway. Place the patient in an AIIR when available, use fit-tested N95 or higher respiratory protection, limit transport, and use a surgical/procedure mask on the patient for necessary transport according to policy.
recognize: Persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis, exposure risk, or compatible imaging can raise suspicion
TB spreads through airborne particles from infectious pulmonary/laryngeal disease
Latent/inactive TB infection is not the same as contagious active pulmonary TB disease
assess: Assess respiratory symptoms, constitutional symptoms, exposure/travel/congregate-setting risks, immune status, and ability to adhere to isolation/treatment
Monitor medication adverse effects and ordered liver/vision or other tests according to the regimen
actions: Initiate airborne precautions for suspected infectious TB according to facility protocol
Limit transport to medically necessary purposes and use source control
Collect ordered sputum specimens correctly and reinforce adherence to the full multidrug treatment plan
diagnostics: NAAT, smear, culture, chest imaging, and immune-based testing have different roles; a positive immune test alone does not prove active pulmonary disease
Culture supports organism identification and susceptibility testing but takes longer than rapid molecular testing
medicationSafety: Isoniazid: hepatotoxicity and neuropathy risk; pyridoxine is used for selected patients
Rifampin/rifampicin: major drug interactions and orange discoloration of body fluids
Ethambutol: visual toxicity requires prompt reporting of vision/color changes
Pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia can occur
teaching: Take every TB medication exactly as prescribed and keep public-health/clinic follow-up
Teach cough etiquette and home isolation instructions provided by the TB program
Explain that stopping early can lead to treatment failure and resistance
scopeAndDelegation: Public-health reporting, isolation discontinuation, and treatment coordination follow federal/state/local TB programs and facility policy. The PN/LVN reinforces the plan and reports adherence barriers/adverse effects; do not independently discontinue isolation.
examTrap: Using only Droplet Precautions or waiting for culture confirmation before protecting staff and other patients from suspected infectious pulmonary TB.
oneLinePearl: Suspected pulmonary TB: airborne now, confirm in parallel.
sourceBasis: CDC Tuberculosis Infection Control and Prevention Guidance

title: Sleep Apnea, Sedation, and Opioids: The Overnight Respiratory Risk
bottomLine: Obstructive sleep apnea increases concern for medication-related respiratory compromise, especially with opioids, benzodiazepines, other sedatives, or residual anesthesia. Monitor ventilation and level of consciousness—not only pain and SpO2—and use prescribed PAP therapy when appropriate.
recognize: OSA clues include loud snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, obesity/airway risk, and existing CPAP/BPAP use
Postoperative or sedated patients may obstruct more when supine or deeply asleep
Supplemental oxygen can maintain SpO2 while hypoventilation and CO2 retention worsen
assess: Assess respiratory rate and quality, sedation level, airway obstruction/snoring, SpO2 and, when ordered, capnography
Review recent opioids/sedatives and whether home PAP should be continued per plan
Reassess after each opioid dose, not only at the next routine vital-sign interval
actions: Use positioning, monitoring, PAP, oxygen, and opioid-sparing strategies as ordered
Hold/clarify or escalate for excessive sedation or respiratory depression according to medication parameters
Activate emergency response and administer naloxone when indicated and authorized
diagnostics: Sleep studies diagnose OSA; bedside monitoring detects acute respiratory compromise but does not replace formal diagnosis
medicationSafety: Combining opioids with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants increases respiratory-depression risk
Naloxone can reverse opioid effect but may wear off before the opioid; continue monitoring for recurrent depression
teaching: Use PAP as prescribed and avoid unapproved alcohol/sedative combinations with opioids
Teach family/patient naloxone use when prescribed for outpatient opioid risk
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN administers and monitors sedating medications within authorized scope and must respond to oversedation immediately. Medication dose changes beyond hold parameters require clarification from the authorized prescriber/protocol.
examTrap: Giving the next opioid because the patient reports severe pain while ignoring that the patient is increasingly difficult to arouse with shallow respirations.
sourceBasis: American Society of Anesthesiologists OSA perioperative guidance
